title: memory-surge-heuristics-tuning-runbook-sketch
incident_summary: Intermittent host memory surges observed across a subset of single-tenant serving hosts between 2024-10-16 and 2024-10-17. Suspected interaction between recent continuous-batching heuristic changes and aggressive prefetching for long-lived KV cache entries, resulting in unbounded KV growth and eventual OOMs on 4 hosts in prod fleet.
body:
Purpose: capture a lightweight post-incident sketch that can evolve into a small runbook and an experimentation plan. This is intentionally pragmatic: short checklist for oncall + where to add short-term mitigations and medium-term telemetry/experiments.

What happened (high level):
- 2024-10-16 03:12 UTC alert spike: multiple hosts in us-west-2 reported memory pressure and OOM kills.
- Impact: ~0.4% of production requests experienced retryable failures over a 27m window; small burst of degraded latency while autoscaler replaced OOMed hosts. No customer data loss.
- Initial triage signal: host memory RSS jumped steadily for ~20–40 minutes before kernel OOMs. The growth correlated with request patterns that include many short-run chains (frequent prompt->call->refill).

Immediate hypotheses we considered:
1) KV cache leak: entries not evicted due to recent change in eviction scoring (continuous batching can extend lifespan of prefetched KV segments).
2) Batching regression: continuous-batching heuristics caused microbatches to accumulate state (per-request contexts) and not be released promptly under certain latency percentiles.
3) Prefetch storm: prefetch backoff misfire where many requests triggered prefetch concurrently and kv-index/shard accounting failed to throttle.

What telemetry we looked at (good signals to add permanently):
- host.mem.rss and host.mem.heap-allocated over time (15s granularity)
- kvcache.local.entry_count and kvcache.local.bytes (per-tenant and per-shard)
- continuous_batch.active_batches and continuous_batch.queue_depth
- request.lifecycle.duration broken by stage (prefetch, decode, generate)
- gc/pagemap churn stats (for languages with managed heaps)
- per-host open file descriptors / number of active eviction goroutines

Quick forensics notes (commands and outputs that helped):
- kubectl logs --since=30m -c serving-runtime <pod> showed repeated prefetch log lines with growing "kv_entry_count=..." values.
- pmap /proc/<pid>/maps + smaps showed a growing anonymous mapping corresponding to the KV arena.
- heap profiles taken with pprof (CPU/heap) at t0 and t+10m showed steady allocation in kv::entry::~Entry path.
- /metrics export showed kvcache_local_entries{shard="s2"} increasing linearly for ~30 minutes before host restart.

Immediate mitigations applied during incident: (what oncall did)
- Rolled out a dynconfig change to temporarily cap kvcache.per_tenant_max_entries=2000 for the affected host pool (fast rollback path).
- Toggled continuous_batch.prefer_local=false (experiment flag) for one canary host to see effect on memory growth.
- If host still OOMing, use orchestrator to drain and reboot host to reinitialize in-memory caches.

Why these mitigations: cap provides immediate bounding of memory, prefer_local flip reduces likelihood of long-lived microbatch state colliding with prefetched KV. Draining prevents cascading OOMs.

Runbook sketch (short checklist for the oncall SRE) - iteration 0:
1) On OOM alert, check host.mem.rss and kvcache.local.bytes for the host.
2) Identify recent dynconfig changes (api: /dynconfig/changes) in last 24h.
3) If kvcache entry count > 50% of per-host memory budget: set dynconfig kvcache.per_tenant_max_entries=2000 (or 50% reduction from current), notify infra.
4) Toggle continuous_batch.prefer_local=false on a single canary host to test regression hypothesis.
5) If memory continues to climb after 10 minutes, cordon+drain host and mark as reboot-needed.
6) After host recovery, compare kvcache.local.entries pre/post and check if evictions are firing.
7) Open an incident ticket SRE-4821 and attach heap profiles and metrics timeseries.

Longer-term run actions (engineering follow-ups):
- Add a hard quota enforcement in serving-runtime: a per-shard/host soft limit + eviction fallbacks. If over quota for >60s, activate aggressive eviction mode and block prefetch.
- Revisit continuous-batching heuristics: add TTL to batch-scoped state and ensure explicit ownership release when microbatch becomes idle for X seconds.
- Add rate-limited global prefetch gate: circuit-breaker that reduces prefetch rate if kvcache growth > threshold.
- Improve observability: add kvcache.eviction_rate, kvcache.prefetch_inflight and histogram of kv_entry_ttl.

Experimentation plan (to prove root cause):
A. Canary A: Flip continuous_batch.prefer_local=false on 10 hosts (low traffic) and observe memory slope for 48h vs control.
B. Canary B: Apply kvcache.per_tenant_max_entries=1000 on 10 hosts and measure request-level latency/95th and error-rate.
C. Synthetic load: run reproducer that simulates short-run chains with prefetch, instrument per-request traces to confirm whether prefetched entries are referenced or orphaned.

Acceptance criteria for root cause:
- If A reduces memory slope significantly without impacting latency: point to batching heuristic interaction.
- If B reduces slope but A does not: point to unbounded kvcache growth as primary cause.
- If both help: interaction likely; we should harden both sides.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are certain tenants triggering more KV retention? (need per-tenant breakdown)
- Is eviction not firing because scoring function changed? (check commit history and tests)
- Could we have a serialization bug in kv-index that duplicates pointers? (requires code audit)

Notes on coordination and safety:
- Dynconfig changes are low-risk but must be accompanied by a rollback plan. Keep a short live channel (SRE + serving-runtime lead) during changes.
- Avoid broad prefer_local flips without canaries; that flag has rollback implications for latency.

Artifact checklist to close incident:
- Upload two heap profiles (one pre-cap and one after reboot) to the ticket.
- Grafana dashboard with new annotations and query for kvcache.local.bytes per-host.
- PR with hard quota and a unit test that simulates enforced eviction.
- Postmortem writeup (template) summarizing root cause and timeline.

TODO (near term):
- Marco: add kvcache.eviction_rate metric by 2024-11-01.
- Lina: prepare canary config flips and run Canary A/B by 2024-11-05.
- Priya: draft runbook checklist and coordinate with SRE rotation for validation.

Snippets of useful diagnostics (copy-paste friendly):
- kubectl exec -it <pod> -c serving-runtime -- /bin/sh -c "curl -s localhost:9090/metrics | grep kvcache_local_entries"
- pprof heap: go tool pprof -http=localhost:6060 /tmp/heap.prof
- tail -n 200 /var/log/serving-runtime/prefetch.log | grep "prefetch" | sed -n '1,200p'

Final thought: the incident looked like a classic multi-factor memory surge (prefetch + batching + eviction scoring) rather than a single-page leak. The quickest durable fix is a small defensive quota and improved telemetry so a follow-on engineering project can make an invariant: "KV cache cannot grow beyond X% of host memory". This doc should evolve into a real runbook after the canaries finish and the hard quota PR lands.

Unresolved: add explicit test harness that runs for 24h with mixed short-run chains and measures kvcache growth. Suggestion: solutions-eng to build a lightweight reproducer container for nightly runs.

Appendix: quick timeline (UTC)
- 2024-10-16 02:58 first anomalous kvcache growth alert (no customer impact)
- 2024-10-16 03:12 three hosts reached OOM and were auto-removed from LB
- 2024-10-16 03:25 SRE triage channel opened, quick cap dynconfig applied
- 2024-10-16 03:40 memory slope reduced on affected hosts
- 2024-10-16 04:10 last host rebooted and incidents quieted

Contact: Priya Nandakumar (oncall SRE lead), Ethan Morales (serving-runtime owner)
notes_summary: Draft runbook + experiment plan for memory surge suspected to be caused by interaction between continuous batching heuristics and KV cache prefetch behavior. Includes quick oncall checklist, mitigation steps, instrumentation improvements and an A/B canary plan.
next_steps: Implement kvcache.eviction_rate metric; run canary experiments; build quota PR; create reproducer; formalize runbook in Confluence.
